questions.text: What is a closure in JavaScript?
options: A function that is passed as an argument to another function
A function that keeps access to the variables of its outer scope after that scope has finished executing
A variable declared with the const keyword
A special built-in object that stores all global variables
questions.explanation: A closure is a function bundled with (and remembering) the variables from its lexical scope, even after the outer function returns.

questions.text: Which statement correctly describes what a closure captures?
options: A copy of the value at the time the inner function is created
A reference to the variable binding, so later changes are visible
Only primitive values, never objects
The outer function's return value
questions.explanation: Closures capture the binding (a reference to the variable), not the value at creation time — that's why the loop trap happens.

questions.text: Why does `var` in the classic loop trap make all closures log the same final value?
options: Because `var` is not hoisted
Because all closures share a single function-scoped `var` binding that ends at the loop's final value
Because closures are optimised away in loops
Because `var` cannot be captured by closures
questions.explanation: `var` is function-scoped, so every iteration uses the same binding; using `let` gives each iteration its own binding.

questions.text: Which is a common use of closures?
options: Encapsulating private state
Creating global variables
Disabling garbage collection
Replacing all classes
questions.explanation: Closures are commonly used to hide internal state and expose only a controlled public API.

questions.text: An arrow function defined inside another function captures which `this`?
options: The global `this`
The `this` of the enclosing (lexical) scope at the point it is written
The `this` of where the function is called
`null` always
questions.explanation: Arrow functions do not have their own `this`; they close over the `this` from the surrounding lexical scope.
